wx.desc: African dust drifted across the Atlantic. The sky turns milky and visibility drops, which makes distances over water hard to judge.

jobs.title: The Starling Needs a Run
paras: Vivienne is grounded by meetings this week, and a jet that sits still gets grumpy. She asks you to take the Starling to Barbados and back to keep it, and you, current. Abe says it counts as homework.
The Starling belongs to Vivienne, so there are no fuel or maintenance bills for you. She pays a flat pilot fee.

jobs.label: Fresh catch

wx.desc: Steady easterly trades, puffy cumulus and endless visibility.

jobs.title: Fresh wahoo to Nevis
paras: A beachfront restaurant on Nevis has a full house tonight and no wahoo on the menu. A fisherman on Antigua landed a good catch this morning, and the coolers are already on the ramp, sweating in the sun.
The chef wants it on ice and on time. It'll smell a bit in the cabin. Dez recommends flying with the vents open and never mentioning it to your next passengers.

bonus.text: Work ATC the whole way (MSFS ATC or VATSIM), from clearance to taxi-in

jobs.title: Urgent: Blood units for Sint Eustatius
paras: The clinic on Sint Eustatius called at short notice: they need six units of O-negative blood, and the regular supply boat isn't due for four days.

A courier is driving the cooler to your aircraft now. The doctor on Sint Eustatius, Dr. Petrov, will meet you planeside. Fast matters, but arriving matters more. Don't let urgency rush your preflight.

bonus.text: Grease it: touch down under 150 fpm

jobs.title: Sightseeing over Antigua
paras: Visitors from Munich booked a scenic flight to see the coastline and reefs of Antigua. They want photos, a few good stories, and to be back in time for dinner.

It's a local flight: depart and return to TAPA. Plan a loop that shows off the sights at a safe altitude, and tell your passengers what they're looking at. They'll remember the pilot who knew the stories.

bonus.text: Show your passengers Saba's cliffs on the way, at a safe altitude

jobs.label: Island mail run

wx.desc: Steady easterly trades, puffy cumulus and endless visibility.

jobs.title: Mail and newspapers to Sint Eustatius
paras: Twice a week the morning mail for Sint Eustatius rides on whatever small airplane is heading that way. Today that's you: canvas sacks of letters, a stack of newspapers, a box of prescription refills and, inevitably, someone's online shopping.
The postmistress on Sint Eustatius, Yvette, will be waiting on the ramp with a hand truck. She keeps a list of pilots who land gently, and she isn't afraid to share it.

job.label: Honeymoon charter

wx.desc: Light winds and a mirror-flat sea. Beautiful, but water landings get tricky.

job.title: Honeymoon to Sint Eustatius
paras: Declan and Owen Moreno from Austin got married three days ago in a barefoot ceremony on Antigua. The second half of the honeymoon is a villa on Sint Eustatius, and they've heard the view from a small airplane beats any ferry.

They've asked for "the scenic way, if it doesn't cost extra." Owen would like the flight to be smooth. Declan would like a low pass over a beach, which you'll politely decline at anything under 1,000 ft.

journal.title: Welcome to Coral Wing
journal.text: Dez claps once when the mains kiss the runway. "Rookie can fly," he tells the whole ramp. Mari will hear about this by lunch.

journal.title: Arrived in St. Martin
journal.text: Fresh license, 62 hours in the logbook, and a trainee job at Coral Wing Air. The trade winds are blowing and the water is every color of blue.

followups.title: Declan & Owen Moreno wants you again
paras: Your last client loved the flight so much they cancelled the airline ticket for their next leg. Their assistant called dispatch: "Same pilot. Same airplane. Tomorrow, or today if possible."
Next stop: Nevis. Repeat clients are how charter pilots stay in business.

If the weather looks bad from the ground, it looks worse from the air. You're allowed to say no.

brief.tip: Mixing up wind direction: METARs and tower winds are true or magnetic depending on source. In the Caribbean the difference is about 13–15°.
